summary: Describes an OSPF extension to reduce periodic flooding of Link State Advertisements in stable networks. Normally OSPF refreshes most LSAs every 30 minutes, and this document proposes making wider use of DoNotAge LSAs to cut that protocol traffic. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo describes a way for OSPF routers to reduce repeat flooding when a topology is stable. Routers still flood changed advertisements immediately, while periodic repeats can be delayed by configuration.

questions: how often does ospf refresh lsas
how does ospf flooding reduction work
how often does ospf force flooding
subtitle: A configurable OSPF extension that reduces flooding of unchanged link-state advertisements.

tldr.problem: OSPF periodically refreshes link-state advertisements even in stable topologies, creating protocol traffic without changed route information.
tldr.mechanism: Routers use the DoNotAge bit for self-originated LSAs and can lengthen the interval for forced flooding; changes to LSA contents are still flooded immediately.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4136 is informational. Flooding reduction is configurable and off by default, and its compatibility behavior relies on the OSPF demand-circuit extensions.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 4136 as Informational and records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo describes OSPF flooding-reduction behavior and configuration.

sections.title: Periodic LSA Refreshes
sections.content:
OSPF requires most Link State Advertisements (LSAs) to be refreshed every 1800 seconds or they expire at 3600 seconds. The RFC says this creates noticeable protocol traffic even when large network topologies are stable.

The proposed extension generalizes use of the DoNotAge bit to reduce that overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPF repeats unchanged route information on a timer. The memo describes how to reduce these repeats in a stable network.

sections.title: Flooding with the DoNotAge Bit
sections.content:
Routers with flooding reduction continue sending hellos and aging their own LSAs in the database, but flood self-originated LSAs with the DoNotAge bit set. They need not re-flood them every 30 minutes; a configured forced-flooding interval can be used instead.

If an LSA's contents change, the router originates and floods an updated LSA immediately. Received DoNotAge LSAs are flooded on normal or flooding-reduction-only interfaces within their flooding scope. On an interface that is also a demand circuit, unchanged LSAs are not re-flooded by that router.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can send unchanged advertisements less often, but they still announce a change right away. They continue sending hello messages to neighbors.

sections.title: Interoperability and Configuration
sections.content:
Routers supporting OSPF demand-circuit extensions can process DoNotAge LSAs and suppress their flooding on demand-circuit interfaces. If routers in the domain or area do not support those extensions, the memo applies the interoperability constraints from RFC 1793.

The feature must be enabled by configuration and is off by default. The flooding-interval default and minimum are 30 minutes; infinity prevents re-flooding unchanged self-originated LSAs. The RFC says the extension creates no new OSPF security issues.
sections.plainLanguage: The feature is off until configured and depends on demand-circuit support for compatibility. Operators can set how often unchanged information is forced out again.
